title: Faith and Circumcision
english: The Lord will not impute sin to the man who is blessed, and this blessing applies to both those who are circumcised and those who are not.
We say that faith was reckoned to Abraham as righteousness, and this is the case because the Lord will not impute sin to him.
The question arises as to how faith was reckoned to Abraham - was it while he was circumcised or while he was still uncircumcised?
The answer is that faith was reckoned to Abraham while he was still uncircumcised, not while he was circumcised.

Abraham received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness that comes from faith, which was present in him even before he was circumcised, so that he might be the father of all who believe, whether they are circumcised or not, and that righteousness might be reckoned to them.

Abraham is also the father of those who are circumcised, but not just those who are physically circumcised - he is also the father of those who follow in the footsteps of his faith, even if they are not circumcised.
In addition to these things, the mystery of God's plan is even more deeply revealed.
The promise that God made to Abraham, that he would be the heir of the world, was not based on the law, but on the righteousness that comes from faith (Romans 4:13).
If those who are under the law were the only ones who could inherit the promise, then faith would be meaningless and the promise would be nullified.
The law brings wrath, and where there is no law, there is no transgression.

Therefore, it is through faith that the promise is confirmed, and it is available to all of Abraham's descendants, not just those who are under the law, but also those who share his faith (Romans 4:16).

As it is written, God said to Abraham, 'I have made you a father of many nations' (Romans 4:17), and Abraham believed in God, who gives life to the dead and calls into being things that do not exist (Romans 4:17).
It is clear that Abraham, who did not yet have circumcision, but was still uncircumcised, received the grace that justifies him through faith.
Those who wish to follow the example of Abraham's faith, even if they are not circumcised, are appointed heirs of the gifts from God.
On the other hand, those who think highly of the law and boast of Abraham as their physical father are not necessarily heirs of the promise.
Abraham is called the father of many nations, even though he was from the nation of Israel, and this is because he became the father of all those who have faith, regardless of their background.
These people have been gathered from every city and region and have become one body in Christ, and they have been called to a spiritual brotherhood.
Although they have come into being from Abraham as Jews, not all of those who are from Israel are truly Israel, and not all of those who are descended from Abraham are his true children.
Rather, it is faith that makes someone a true child of Abraham, and this is the case for those who believe, whether they are circumcised or not.
The promise was made to Abraham while he was still uncircumcised, and the justifying grace was given to him at that time, according to the faith of the holy ones.

You hear it being confirmed that to Abraham, who did not yet have circumcision, but was still in uncircumcision, the grace that justifies him through faith was given, and that those who wish to follow the example of the faith of the ancestor Abraham in uncircumcision are appointed heirs of the gifts from God, and not those who are accustomed to think highly of the shadow served through Moses, and boast of Abraham as their physical father, who is named the father of many nations, although he is of one nation, Israel, and even if it were extended to an immeasurable multitude, because he became the father of those who have come to faith, who have been gathered from every city and region, and have become one body in Christ, and have been called to a spiritual brotherhood.
And the fact that of the in faith…
translator_notes: The phrase 'Ὅτι δὲ τῆς ἐν πίστει δ' is a fragment and appears to be cut off; translated literally as 'And the fact that of the in faith' with a trailing ellipsis.
The Greek text may be fragmented, and some sentences may be cut off at the end.
The allusion to Romans 4:13 is based on the reference to the promise of inheriting the world.
The allusion to Romans 4:17 is based on the reference to Abraham being made the father of many nations and his faith in God who gives life to the dead.

title: Spiritual Circumcision
english: You see that the type of circumcision in spirit and truth was shown beforehand in the flesh. It is done on the eighth day, on which Christ rose from the dead. When Christ rose, having broken the power of death, he also gave the firstfruits of the Holy Spirit to the holy disciples. For he breathed on them, saying: 'Receive the Holy Spirit.'

The wise John also agrees, saying: 'The Holy Spirit was not yet given, because Jesus was not yet glorified.' He was glorified, having risen from the dead on the eighth day. Therefore, the Spirit was also poured out on us, and we are circumcised with a circumcision that is not made by hands and is spiritual. This manner of circumcision is pleasing to God. And the divine Paul says: 'For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is circumcision that which is outward in the flesh, but he is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is that of the heart, in the Spirit, not in the letter' (Romans 2:28-29). Whose praise is not from men, but from God.

It was already time to dismiss the Jewish synagogue and assembly, and to make the people from it a separate entity, as it were, of the promise. And indeed, the Scripture indicates that it will return at the proper time and will be accepted, and it will attain the gentleness from above and from the Father, recognizing the Savior and Redeemer of all. The children, namely Isaac and Ishmael, were playing with each other, and it seems that their play was a kind of chasing. Ishmael was chasing, and Isaac was being chased. But the mind of the free woman, namely Sarah, was grieved by this, and she said to Abraham: 'Cast out this slave woman and her son' (Genesis 21:10), because the son of the slave woman would not inherit with her son Isaac. And Abraham was not at peace with this word, but he heard from God that he should obey Sarah's words. So he provided Hagar with bread and water and told her to leave with the child of the mistress's household. And she went away, weeping and lamenting, but she wandered in the wilderness, and when the child was in danger and crying, God opened…

As the child's situation became more desperate, God's intervention became more necessary. The dismissal of Hagar and her son was a pivotal moment in the story, one that would have far-reaching consequences. The fact that Ishmael was chasing Isaac, and that Sarah was grieved by this, suggests that there was already tension between the two women and their sons. The quote from Genesis 21:10, 'Cast out this slave woman and her son,' highlights the conflict between Sarah and Hagar, and sets the stage for the events that will unfold. The gentleness from above and from the Father, which the Scripture promises, will be essential for the characters as they navigate this difficult situation.
translator_notes: The Greek text begins mid-sentence: 'μου διεσκέδασεν.'
The translation of 'ἐπιστρέψει' as 'will return' is based on the future tense indicating a future action.
The translation of 'τεύξεται' as 'will attain' is based on the future tense indicating a future action.

title: Faith and the Law
english: The promise remains, but it serves as a tutor, bringing us near to the calling through faith.
This tutorship is necessary because it shows the weakness of those who have already entered, and it proves that the grace through faith and the justification in Christ are essential for all.
Paul says again, 'Brothers, I speak in human terms: even though it is a human covenant that has been confirmed, no one annuls it or adds to it.' (Galatians 3:15)
The promises were made to Abraham and his seed.
It does not say 'and to seeds,' as if referring to many, but 'and to your seed,' as referring to one, and your seed is Christ.
This is a covenant confirmed by God.
The law, which came into being 430 years later, does not nullify the promise.
If the inheritance were from the law, it would no longer be from a promise, but God granted it to Abraham by a promise.

Paul adds the reason for the law's introduction, saying it was added because of transgressions until the seed should come to whom the promise was made, having been ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator.
Now a mediator is not for one party only, but God is one.
Is the law then against the promises of God? Certainly not!
For if a law had been given that could impart life, then righteousness would indeed be from the law.
But Scripture has confined all things under sin, so that the promise by faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe.
Before faith came, we were held under the law, enclosed until the glory that is about to be revealed.
Thus the law has become our tutor to lead us to Christ, that we might be justified by faith.
But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a tutor.
For you are all sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus.
The law was a demonstration of the weakness of those being tutored, rather than a demonstration of transgressions and sin.
Where there is no law, neither is there transgression.
If it had not been for the law, I would not have known sin.
But when the commandment came, sin came alive and I died.
Before the law, sin was in the world, but sin is not charged when there is no law.
For the law produces wrath.

The law was a tutor leading to Christ, convicting transgressors and teaching those on earth that it is impossible to escape from the law into sin, and that the person weakened by sin needs salvation through Christ, who justifies through faith and mercy.
translator_notes: The source ends with 'καὶ ἐν Χριστῷ δραμούσης χάρι', which appears to be cut off; rendered literally with trailing ellipsis.

The phrase 'the law was a demonstration of the weakness of those being tutored, rather than a demonstration of transgressions and sin' from the gloss is not in the source and is omitted per instructions.
